Someone asked: "My son just turned 22. What advice would you give him?"

Firstly, I don't give advice to people who aren't asking for it. So I probably wouldn't force my advice down your 22-year-old son's throat.

So from 22 to 25, just try loads of things. Internships. Working for a small business. Random hobbies and side projects. Try learning the skills to make money independently on the internet.

And make sure you are creating more than you are consuming. Creating doesn't have to mean content. It can mean any form of making stuff and putting it out into the world.

Paul Graham has a great essay about finding work you love, and one of his guiding principles is "always be producing." The people who stumble into interesting careers tend to produce a lot. Most 22-year-olds I know spend 10 hours a day consuming content other people made.

Everything I'm building is exciting...That's exactly the problem.

Like a lot of creatives, I diverge. I explore. I chase the next shiny object because new territory is energizing. But at some point, everything on your plate is competing for the same finite energy.

When I was at @thechrisdo's business intensive at Casa Dojo, each of us got one hour of focused coaching on one big problem. Mine was this one: too many directions, and not enough clarity on which one to lean into.

So Chris had me lay out every initiative I'm running. Then he asked some questions that stood out for me:

1. Which one naturally energizes me?
2. Which one is the most scalable and sellable?
3. Which one supports my foundational income and cash flow?

After reflecting, I realized that those can be three different answers.

The one that lights me up isn't always the one that pays the bills. And the one that could sell someday might not be the one I want to spend my days on.

This is difficult because there's no single right answer... it depends on the season you're in.

- A season of profitability and scalability? Lean into what can grow and sell.
- A season of lifestyle and flexibility? Protect your energy and your time.
- A season of long-term building toward an exit? Invest in what compounds, even when it doesn't pay yet.

Although more ideas and more discipline would help, it wasn't what I needed. I needed someone to pull everything onto the table and reflect it back so I could see it clearly.

This is the biggest benefit that I've found in coaching and to have Chris filter my situation through his experience and lens was a huge privilege.

If you're a creative with too many things going on, try this: list everything you're working on, run each one through those three questions, and ask which season you're actually in.

If you chase after money, it has a funny way of avoiding you.

At least, that's what I've found in my career.

Instead, I'd much rather focus on something better:

Big, painful, miserable problems.

I started learning how to solve these problems back in 2009 in my startup days, and quickly figured out how valuable that was.

Solve one painful problem? Here's some money.
Solve another one? Here's more.
Keep solving them? Here's a boatload.

When you can save people money or time (or both) AND help them sleep better at night, you have incredible earning potential.

So work on that skill ferociously.

Here's how I do it:

1. Hypothesize

When you see a big problem, try to write down every single reason you think it might be happening. Guess. Jot every single thing you can think of.

2. Rank

Stack rank them from most likely to least likely to be the culprit. Start by cutting everything except the top 2 or 3.

3. Isolate

Starting with your most likely, figure out how to isolate your hypothesis and measure it effectively.

4. Prove or disprove

Don't guide the data. Let the data guide you. Were you right? Wrong? Talk to people as well. Qualitative and quantitative feedback are useful.

5. Install

Once you've figured out the actual fix, install it. Then move on to the next problem.

Congrats...you're on your way to being hyper valuable.

The worst thing in the world is getting fired without a backup plan.

$200,000 take-home pay one day.
$0 the next day.

That's why planning for the worst, while working hard to prevent it, is a great 1-2 punch.

1. Make some noise

Get online daily and share how you think about your industry. Let people see your name and face and become synonymous with something.

2. Build a network

Once you've made a little noise, jump into DMs. Invite people to connect. Grab coffee. Meet on Zoom. Help people. It's all about who you know.

3. Show off your expertise

At some point, don't just make noise. Translate noise into value. What have you helped your company accomplish? Toot your own horn.

4. Collect testimonials

If colleagues, managers, and peers like your work, ask them to write a little something about it. Put it on LinkedIn. Put it on your website. Show off what other people think about you.

5. Connect people

Lastly, make mutually beneficial connections.

Once people feel like you've helped them out, they'll remember you when opportunities show up.

Your expertise.

Easy expectations.

Do the opposite.

Find people who are better than you and make yourself useful to them.

Take on some work that scares you a little.

Become the person who can be trusted with expensive, painful problems.

And then stay long enough to actually get good.

You'll build a reputation long before you desperately need one.

Because later, freedom gets much easier when you already have experience people value, people who trust you, and proof that you can deliver.

That's how I spent the first half of my career.

The second half was figuring out how to turn everything I learned into income I controlled without creating another life-consuming job.

Most entrepreneurs try to build a business first and then cram their life around it.

I think that's a mistake.

Before you build anything, you should decide what your business is going to make possible in your life.

Here are some important questions to think through:

How many hours do you want to work?
How much income is actually enough?
Do you want weekends protected?
Do you want employees?
Do you want meetings?
Do you want to travel?

Those answers should help shape the business model that you eventually choose.

Because the answers affect what you sell, how you price it, how much complexity you install, and what kinds of customers you avoid.

You can build a "great" business and still build the wrong one for the life you want to live.

So define your life first.
Then build the business that supports it.

That was how I approached my one-person business, and it forced me to get excellent at a handful of skills:

Choosing the best work for me.
Keeping everything overly simple.
Protecting my time (especially weekends).
Creating predictable income with automation.

Being uncomfortable with self-promotion is expensive.

But you don't need to become obnoxious.

You do need to get good at three things:

1. Show your work.

Talk about what you're building, what you're learning, what worked, and what failed. Be open, honest, and helpful.

2. Make your value extremely obvious.

Explain the problem you solve and show the result. Make it simple. A 6th-grader should be able to understand it.
